items.title: L6: Reading a conditional offer
items.source: Civil Service Jobs guidance; HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard (GOV.UK)
items.body:
A conditional offer says the department will employ you if certain conditions are met. The conditions usually include satisfactory baseline checks (the BPSS), any security clearance the role needs, and references or other checks named in the letter. Until every condition is met, the offer is not final. Departments commonly say the start date is only confirmed once checks are cleared, so it is sensible not to hand in your notice, or commit to a big financial step that depends on the job, until you have it in writing that the conditions are met or the department has confirmed that you can start.

The checks team will send forms and ask for documents by a deadline. Most delays come from slow replies, missing documents or incomplete forms, so answer quickly and completely. If your situation changes between offer and start (a new address, a new caution, a second job, a change of name), tell the team rather than waiting to be asked. An offer can be withdrawn if checks are unsatisfactory, but it can also be withdrawn if you gave false or incomplete information, even where the true facts would not have mattered.

Some roles need higher clearance, which takes longer than the baseline checks. Some departments let new starters begin with restricted access while clearance is pending, but this depends on the role and department, so ask rather than assume.

questions.prompt: Maria has a conditional offer. Her BPSS is cleared but SC vetting has not started, and her employer wants a notice date. What is the sensible step?

options.text: Ask the recruiting team in writing whether a start date is confirmed and whether she can start while clearance is still pending, before she gives notice
Resign now, because once the BPSS is cleared the rest of the process is a formality and offers are rarely withdrawn at that stage
Wait until her first day to tell her employer, so that her current job stays safe in case the offer falls through at the last moment
Give her employer a notice date based on the start date in the original advert, since the department chose it when it published the post

questions.hint: Conditions can remain outstanding after the BPSS, so confirm the start position before committing.

questions.prompt: Which situation is the clearest example of an offer condition that has not yet been met?

options.text: The advert named one team, and the letter names a different team in the same building as your new base
The pay band in the letter matches the advert, and you have not yet been told your first day's timetable
The letter says the offer depends on SC clearance, and no vetting decision has been issued yet
The letter arrived by email, and the department has not yet received a signed paper copy back from you

questions.hint: A condition stays unmet until the decision or check is actually complete.

questions.prompt: Dev's forms are due in a week. He is on holiday and plans to complete them on his return two weeks later. What is the likely effect?

options.text: His offer is withdrawn the moment any deadline is missed, whatever the reason, because the rules allow no flexibility
His check will probably be delayed, because it cannot progress without his forms, and his start date may move as a result
Nothing at all, because the deadline is advisory and departments wait for everyone to return from leave before they begin checks
His start date moves earlier, because late forms are taken as a sign that the person is available to begin sooner

questions.hint: Most delays come from late paperwork, so deadlines matter and problems should be raised early.

questions.prompt: Between accepting and starting, Sam takes up a second job at weekends. What should Sam do?

options.text: Say nothing until the probation review, because the job began after the offer was accepted and so cannot affect the checks already done
Mention it only if a later form asks directly about outside work, since volunteering information is not expected
Give up the weekend job quietly so that there is nothing to mention and the question never arises
Tell the checks team or line manager so the change can be recorded

questions.hint: Changes between offer and start should be raised, not left for someone to find.

questions.prompt: Priya wrongly wrote that she holds a degree the role does not require. What risk does the error create?

options.text: The offer can still be withdrawn, because false information is a problem even where the true fact did not matter
None, because the degree was not a requirement and so the claim cannot affect the outcome of the checks or the offer
A risk to her pay band only, since a degree claim is used to set grading and has no bearing on honesty
None until she starts, because the honesty rules apply only once the contract of employment has begun

questions.hint: Honesty is judged separately from whether the false fact mattered.

questions.prompt: Why might a department let a new starter begin before vetting is complete?

options.text: Because the clearance level is chosen after the person has shown their ability in the job rather than before it
Restricted access can let them begin work while sensitive material stays out of reach until the vetting decision arrives
Because the baseline checks already prove suitability for access at every level, so vetting only confirms them
Because clearance is a formality that can be completed at any point during the first year without consequence

questions.hint: Starting with limited access is a departmental choice, not a right.

questions.prompt: An offer depends on satisfactory references, and your previous manager is hard to reach. What should you do?

options.text: Wait quietly, because chasing a referee is the department's job rather than the candidate's and any approach could look like interference
Write the reference yourself and ask the manager to sign it, as this saves the manager time and gets you cleared sooner
Leave the reference blank, on the basis that a missing reference is treated as satisfactory once the other checks have passed
Tell the checks team and offer another person, such as a senior colleague, who can confirm the work

questions.hint: Candidates help by offering an alternative referee, not by writing or ignoring the reference.

questions.prompt: A caller says they are from HR and asks you to text your passport number for the checks. What is the right response?

options.text: Send it, because a caller who knows your job title and start date must be genuine and would not otherwise have the details
Send it but ask them to promise to delete it, which is enough protection for a document number sent by text
Send nothing by text, and confirm the request first using the contact details named in your offer letter or on the official site
Send only the first half of the number now and the rest once they have confirmed who they are by phone

questions.hint: Sensitive details go through the secure route the department has given, not to unverified callers.

questions.prompt: A friend says, 'You have the job; the letter is just paperwork.' Based on the letter, what is the best reply?

options.text: The offer is conditional, so the job is not secure until the named checks are complete
That is right, since everyone who receives an offer letter has by then already passed all of the checks it mentions
That is right once references are in, because only the security checks can still go wrong at this stage
It depends on whether the friend works in government, because insiders understand which letters are binding

questions.hint: A conditional offer is exactly that: the conditions must be satisfied before the job is final.

questions.prompt: A letter promises a start date 'subject to clearance', and clearance is delayed. Who decides what happens to the date?

options.text: The vetting service, which sets start dates for every Civil Service post that depends on clearance
The candidate's previous employer, who may release staff only on the day clearance is granted
The employing department, which owns the start date and will usually confirm any change to it in writing
The candidate, who may choose any later date and simply let the department know when they will arrive

questions.hint: The employing department owns the start date and normally communicates changes.

items.title: L6: Identity evidence in awkward cases
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard; GOV.UK right to work guidance
items.body:
The BPSS asks you to prove who you are. The aim is to be confident that you are a real person, that you are the person you say you are, and that the name and date of birth you give belong to one identity. Departments usually ask for a combination of documents: one showing photographic identity (such as a passport or driving licence), and others showing your name and current address (such as a bank statement or utility bill). Exact lists are set by each department, so always follow the list you are sent.

Awkward cases are common. If your name has changed through marriage or by deed poll, you normally need a document linking the names, such as a marriage certificate or the deed. If your address on a licence is out of date, you use other recent documents that show the current address and, where you can, update the licence record. If a document has expired, ask the checks team whether it can be accepted or if you need to renew it. Never alter a document, borrow one or submit one that is not yours.

Checking staff look for consistency. The same name, date of birth and address pattern across documents is reassuring. Differences are not automatically a problem, but they need an explanation. A short plain note with supporting evidence is better than hoping nobody notices.

questions.prompt: Amira's passport is in her birth name but her bank statements use her married name. What should she supply to go with them?

options.text: Nothing further, because checkers will assume that a change of name has taken place when the names differ
A signed note from a friend saying that the two names belong to the same person and that they have known her for years
A new bank statement in her birth name from an account opened specially for the purpose of the check
A marriage certificate or similar official document linking the names

questions.hint: A linking document ties two names to one identity; a casual note or a new account does not.

questions.prompt: Which combination of evidence is closest to what departments usually ask for?

options.text: A recent payslip alone, because it shows employment, name and address together on a single document
One photographic identity document, such as a passport, plus other documents showing your name and current address
Two photographic documents, since a second photograph is stronger evidence than any proof of address
A single utility bill, because it combines name, address and the account holder's signature on one page

questions.hint: The usual pattern pairs photo identity with proof of name and address.

questions.prompt: Leon's driving licence shows an address he left two years ago. What is the sensible step?

options.text: Leave the licence out and say nothing about the mismatch, so that no question about addresses is raised
Submit the licence as it is and hope nobody notices, because the photograph is the part checkers rely on
Cross out the old address and write the new one on the licence by hand, since that shows he is being open about the change
Give other recent documents showing his current address and mention the licence

questions.hint: Explain the difference and give current-address evidence; never alter a document.

questions.prompt: Why do checkers look for consistency across a person's documents?

options.text: A consistent name, date of birth and address pattern across the documents supports the case that they all belong to one genuine identity
Matching layouts and fonts show that all the documents were issued by the same authority and are therefore genuine
Any inconsistency is penalised automatically by refusing the offer, so checkers look for it first
Consistent documents show that the person has stayed with one employer for many years and is therefore reliable

questions.hint: Consistency supports a genuine identity; differences need explaining.

questions.prompt: Chen's passport expires next month, before his start date. What should he do?

options.text: Leave the passport out and send a library card in its place, as any card with a photograph will do
Use his sister's valid passport instead, since she has a similar name and it will be accepted without question
Tell the checks team and ask whether to renew first or whether it will be accepted
Wait until after he starts, because the passport only matters for the first check and later expiry is irrelevant

questions.hint: Expiry affects acceptance, so ask; never substitute somebody else's document.

questions.prompt: Which action is clearly unacceptable when providing identity evidence?

options.text: Providing a deed poll to explain a change of surname which was made some years ago
Submitting a genuine document that belongs to a relative with a similar name, in place of your own
Presenting an original at an appointment arranged by the department rather than posting it
Asking the checks team which of two possible documents they would prefer to see

questions.hint: Documents must be your own and unaltered.

questions.prompt: Zara has lived at four addresses in three years. What is the best approach to proving her address?

options.text: Leave the address blank, since addresses matter only for security clearance and not for the baseline checks
Give the address she liked best and leave out the others, as only one address is ever needed
Follow the department's list, give the most recent evidence and explain the moves if asked
Give only the oldest address, since it has the longest paper trail and so is the easiest to verify

questions.hint: Give honest, current evidence and explain moves.

questions.prompt: A checker queries a small difference in how your middle name is spelt on two documents. What is the helpful response?

options.text: Explain the difference plainly and offer evidence, such as a birth certificate, that shows the correct spelling
Insist there is no difference and refuse to discuss it, because queries from checkers are only a pressure tactic
Withdraw your application, because any query from a checker means that the application will certainly be refused
Change the spelling on the form to match whichever document looks newer, so that all the paperwork agrees

questions.hint: Small differences can usually be resolved with a short explanation and evidence.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the identity part of the BPSS?

options.text: To confirm the applicant's qualifications and professional memberships so that the grading of the role is correct
To be confident that the applicant is who they say they are
To establish whether the applicant has previously worked in government and should be given credit for that service
To decide the applicant's pay band by looking at the address and employment shown on their documents

questions.hint: Identity checking establishes who the person is, not qualifications or pay.

questions.prompt: A department asks for originals rather than photocopies. What is the most likely reason?

options.text: Originals are asked for only from people who are applying for the higher levels of clearance
Photocopies are banned by law in every Civil Service recruitment process and so cannot be accepted
Originals are cheaper for the department to file and store than a set of copies
Originals can be examined for features such as paper, print and watermarks that photocopies lose

questions.hint: Originals are harder to forge and show features copies cannot.

items.title: L6: Accounting for the last three years
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard; Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body:
The BPSS employment check usually covers the past three years. The department wants to know what you were doing throughout, not only which jobs you held. Every period should be accounted for: employment, self-employment, study, unemployment, travel, caring or illness. You will normally be asked for the names of employers or other people who can confirm the periods, and for dates.

Confirmation depends on the situation. For employees, a previous employer or HR can usually confirm dates and job title. For self-employed periods, evidence might be a client, an accountant, or tax records. For study, a college can confirm enrolment. For unemployment or caring, departments often accept an honest explanation and, where possible, someone who knew you at the time. For time abroad, evidence may include travel documents and an overseas employer or institution. The method varies, so follow the department's guidance.

Gaps are not a problem in themselves. Hiding or inventing something is. If a former employer has closed, say so and offer alternative evidence such as payslips or a contract. If you worked under a different name, say so. If you are unsure about exact dates, give your best accurate estimate and say it is approximate; do not guess confidently.

Where information on your form differs from what the previous employer says, the checker may ask you to explain. A prompt, honest answer usually resolves it.

questions.prompt: Hana was self-employed as a decorator for two years. Which is the most suitable evidence of that period?

options.text: A client who can confirm the work, or an accountant or tax records, with dates
A note from a friend saying that she was always busy and never short of customers over those two years
Nothing, because self-employment cannot be checked and so departments leave it out of the history altogether
A reference from a line manager in her new department, who has seen her work only since she was recruited

questions.hint: Self-employment can be supported by clients, accountants or tax records.

questions.prompt: Tomas spent nine months caring for a relative. How should he treat that period?

options.text: Leave it out, because caring is not employment and the form asks only about jobs and paid work
State it honestly with dates, and name someone who knew about the arrangement at the time if he can
Delay sending the form until the period falls outside the three years that the department checks
Describe it as a job so that there is no gap on the form, since gaps count against applicants

questions.hint: All periods should be accounted for, and an honest account of caring is normally acceptable.

questions.prompt: Which statement about gaps in an employment history is the most accurate?

options.text: A gap longer than a month leads automatically to the offer being withdrawn, however it is explained
Gaps matter only to security clearance and are of no interest to the baseline employment check
A gap is not a problem by itself, but it should be explained honestly
A gap should be covered by describing the time as freelance work, which is always accepted without evidence

questions.hint: The issue is hidden or invented information, not the gap.

questions.prompt: Your last employer closed down a year ago. What should you tell the checks team?

options.text: Nothing, since a closed company cannot be checked and so there is no point in listing it
That you will arrange a reference for it once you have started work and settled into the new job
That you never worked there, because that avoids a complicated check which could delay your start
That it has closed, with other evidence such as a contract, payslips or a former colleague

questions.hint: If the employer is gone, say so and offer other evidence of the dates.

questions.prompt: You worked abroad for 18 months within the check period. What is the likely approach?

options.text: Ask a friend in the UK to say you were living locally, so that the history appears continuous
Give the employer's details and be ready to show travel records or other supporting documents
Say you were unemployed, because that is simpler to explain than a long period spent overseas
Leave the period out, since a UK department has no way of contacting an overseas employer

questions.hint: Overseas periods still need to be accounted for, with evidence where available.

questions.prompt: Ella cannot remember the exact month a job began. What should she write?

options.text: A confident date that sounds right, to avoid looking uncertain in front of the checker
The start date from the original job advert she once saw, whether or not it is correct
Her best estimate, clearly marked as approximate, after she has checked any contract, payslip or email that could narrow it down
Nothing for that job, because uncertain dates cannot be used and the entry would only cause confusion

questions.hint: Estimates are acceptable when flagged as such; false certainty is not.

questions.prompt: Your form says you left a job in March but the former employer's records say May. What is the best response?

options.text: Check your own documents and explain the difference promptly if asked
Change your form quietly to match the employer's date, so that the two records agree before anyone looks
Withdraw from the process, because a mismatch between records always ends an application at this stage
Insist the employer is wrong and refuse to discuss it, because your own recollection must be the more reliable

questions.hint: Differences are usually resolved with evidence and a prompt honest explanation.

questions.prompt: You worked under a previous surname for part of the check period. What should you do?

options.text: Ask the former employer to update its records to your new name before the check is carried out
List the job twice, once under each surname, so that every possible record is covered by the form
Use only your current surname throughout, as the old one is not relevant to your present identity
Tell the checks team and supply the document linking the names, so that records held under the earlier name can be traced

questions.hint: Name changes should be disclosed so records under the old name can be linked.

questions.prompt: What is the main reason for checking employment history?

options.text: To count how many promotions the person has had, which helps the department to decide on the right grade
To confirm that the person has always worked in the public sector, which is a condition of most posts
To work out the salary the person should be paid in the new role, based on their previous employers
To confirm that the person's account of how they spent their time is honest and consistent

questions.hint: The check tests honesty and consistency of the account.

questions.prompt: Which of these would a candidate normally not need to account for in the BPSS employment check?

options.text: A job that ended some time before the start of the check period and is therefore outside it
A period of self-employment within the check period, without any employer
A period of study within the check period, such as a part-time course
A period of unemployment within the check period, with no paid work at all

questions.hint: Everything within the window needs accounting for; earlier jobs fall outside it.

items.title: L6: Declaring convictions and cautions
items.source: Rehabilitation of Offenders Act 1974 (legislation.gov.uk); HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard
items.body:
The criminal record part of the BPSS asks about unspent convictions. Under the Rehabilitation of Offenders Act 1974, most convictions become spent after a rehabilitation period, which depends on the sentence given rather than on the offence itself. Once a conviction is spent, you are generally treated as if it had not happened, and for the BPSS you are normally not required to declare it. Longer sentences take longer to become spent, and the most serious sentences never become spent.

Cautions are treated in a similar way, with their own rules about when they become spent. Rules differ slightly between England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, so follow the guidance on the form and ask if unsure. Some roles are exempt from the Act, which means that questions about spent convictions can be asked. The exemption applies to the role, not to the individual, and the application form will normally say so. For higher security clearances the questions are wider, so read each form carefully and answer exactly what is asked.

The core rule is honesty. If you have an unspent conviction, declare it fully on the form rather than waiting to be found. A declared conviction is considered in context, including the offence, how long ago and what you have done since. A concealed one is judged as a lack of honesty, which is often worse than the conviction. If you are unsure whether something is spent, check the rehabilitation rules or ask the checks team before you submit.

questions.prompt: What mainly determines how long a conviction takes to become spent?

options.text: The age of the person at the time of applying for a job, because younger people are treated more leniently
The department being applied to, which sets its own period for each type of post
The sentence given
The name of the offence, since each offence has a fixed period set out in the Act

questions.hint: Under the 1974 Act, the sentence decides the rehabilitation period, not the label of the offence.

questions.prompt: Kofi has a spent conviction and the BPSS form asks only about unspent convictions. What does he do?

options.text: Ask a friend to answer the question for him, since the answer may be seen as a legal matter
Answer the question exactly as asked, which means not declaring a conviction that is spent and falls outside it
Wait for the interview and mention it casually, so that it does not look as if he is hiding it
Declare it anyway, on the basis that more detail is always safer and cannot count against him

questions.hint: For a standard role, spent convictions are not declared unless the form asks about them.

questions.prompt: Rhys has an unspent conviction. When is the best time to declare it?

options.text: On the form, fully, where it is asked for
After the offer is confirmed, when it can no longer be withdrawn on the strength of the new information
On his first day, when meeting his manager, so that the news is delivered in person
Only if the checker finds it in the records, as volunteering it would draw attention that is not needed

questions.hint: Declaring on the form is honest and lets the department weigh it in context.

questions.prompt: Why can concealing an unspent conviction be more damaging than the conviction itself?

options.text: Concealment is a separate offence under the Official Secrets Act, which carries its own penalty
The department must reject anyone with a conviction, so concealment is a way to improve the chances
Concealed convictions are always the more serious offences, which is why people have a reason to hide them
It shows a lack of honesty, which is a core concern of the checks and can weigh more than the conviction

questions.hint: The checks value honesty highly, so concealing can outweigh the underlying fact.

questions.prompt: What does it mean when a role is exempt from the Rehabilitation of Offenders Act?

options.text: The role has a shorter application process, because the usual rehabilitation periods have been removed
The role requires no criminal record check of any kind, because the Act is not applied to it
Questions about spent convictions may be asked for that role, and the form will normally say so
The role is open only to people with no convictions at all, spent or unspent, from any period

questions.hint: Exemptions attach to the role and allow questions about spent convictions.

questions.prompt: Which statement about cautions is the most accurate?

options.text: They remain unspent for the whole of someone's life, which is why they are always declared
They have their own rules for when they become spent, which can differ across the UK nations
They have to be declared only by people who have no convictions, since the two are alternatives
They are never relevant to any application, because a caution is not a conviction in law

questions.hint: Cautions follow similar principles with their own timing.

questions.prompt: Nadia cannot tell whether an old conviction is spent. What is the best step?

options.text: Assume that it is spent and leave it out, since declaring too much may count against her
Wait until clearance and ask the vetting officer then, when she is sure of the position
Describe it in detail anyway, even if it turns out to be spent, as this is the safest course
Check the rehabilitation rules or ask the checks team before she submits

questions.hint: Uncertainty should be resolved before submission by checking the rules or asking.

questions.prompt: What generally happens when someone declares an unspent conviction honestly?

options.text: It is considered in context, including how long ago it was and what has happened since
The department tells the person's referees, so that they can comment on the circumstances
The conviction is removed from their record by the department as a reward for openness
The offer is withdrawn automatically, as the checks allow no discretion once a conviction is disclosed

questions.hint: A declared conviction is assessed in context, not automatically disqualifying.

questions.prompt: How does a higher-level clearance form compare with the BPSS form?

options.text: The questions are identical unless the person has held clearance before, in which case they are shorter
The questions are wider than on the BPSS, so each form's wording should be read carefully and answered as asked
The questions are identical, since every security form is based on the same wording and scope
The questions are narrower, because anyone applying for clearance has already passed the baseline

questions.hint: Higher clearance explores more areas, so answer exactly what each form asks.

questions.prompt: What is true of the most serious sentences under the 1974 Act?

options.text: They become spent after exactly one year, in the same way as every other sentence under the Act
They become spent when the person changes their name by deed poll and so starts a new record
They never become spent
They become spent once the person has joined the Civil Service and completed probation

questions.hint: The most serious sentences are outside the spent regime altogether.

items.title: L6: Right to work checks in practice
items.source: GOV.UK: Check a job applicant's right to work; Immigration, Asylum and Nationality Act 2006
items.body:
Employers in the UK must check that every person they employ has the right to work, before they start. This applies to everyone, including British citizens, so being asked to prove it does not mean you are under suspicion. The check protects the employer: carrying it out correctly gives them a statutory excuse against a civil penalty if it later turns out the person was not allowed to work.

There are two main routes. People with a British or Irish passport (or certain other documents) can show the original document in person or through an approved digital identity service. People with immigration permission, such as a visa or settled status, usually prove it online by giving the employer a share code from the Home Office service and their date of birth. The employer uses the code to view the status and then checks that the photo and details match the person in front of them.

The employer keeps a record, for example a copy of the check result, dated and stored securely. If permission to work has an end date, the employer must carry out a follow-up check before it ends. Employees have a duty to be honest about changes to their status.

If a person has applied to extend their permission before it runs out, special rules may apply, and the employer should follow the Home Office guidance rather than assume. Right to work is separate from the Civil Service Nationality Rules: a person may have the right to work but not be eligible for a particular post.

questions.prompt: Why is a British citizen also asked to prove the right to work?

options.text: Checks are voluntary for people from outside the UK, so British citizens make up the main checked group
British citizens are statistically more likely to present false documents, so they are checked more carefully
Every new employee must be checked in the same way, so that nobody is judged by assumption
The check is a test of loyalty to the Civil Service and is carried out for everyone in the same way

questions.hint: Checking everyone consistently protects the employer and avoids assumptions.

questions.prompt: What is a share code used for?

options.text: Letting an employer see someone's security clearance level before they join the department
Letting an employer view someone's criminal record held on the police national computer
Sharing a National Insurance number with payroll so that tax can be set up before the first pay day
Letting an employer view someone's immigration status online through the Home Office service

questions.hint: Share codes give controlled online access to immigration status for right to work checks.

questions.prompt: Parveen's permission to work ends in four months and her contract runs for a year. What must the employer do?

options.text: Carry out a follow-up check before her permission ends
Ask her to arrange a check with her previous employer, who has the original document on file
Wait until she has left and then record the date on which her permission actually came to an end
Treat the first check as valid for the whole contract, since a check is a one-off requirement

questions.hint: Time-limited permission requires a follow-up check before the end date.

questions.prompt: What does a correctly performed check give the employer?

options.text: Permission to share the employee's documents with other employers who might wish to hire them
A statutory excuse against a civil penalty if the person turns out not to be allowed to work
A right to dismiss the employee at any time without notice if their status later changes
A guarantee that the employee will pass any security clearance needed for the role they are joining

questions.hint: A properly done check gives a defence against civil penalties, nothing broader.

questions.prompt: Daniel shows his passport at interview and the employer only glances at it. Is that enough?

options.text: Not enough, because only a visa or a share code can be used for the purposes of a right to work check
Not enough: the employer must check the passport is genuine, that Daniel matches the photograph, and keep a dated record
Enough, because a glance is all that is needed for a British passport and the rest is formality
Enough, because the offer letter already states his nationality and that has been accepted by the employer

questions.hint: A proper check includes examining authenticity, matching the person and keeping a record.

questions.prompt: Which is a correct description of the link between right to work and the Civil Service Nationality Rules?

options.text: The nationality rules replace the right to work check in the Civil Service, which therefore does not need it
They are the same check, so a person who passes one has automatically passed the other
They are separate: someone can have the right to work but not meet the rules for a particular post
The right to work check is needed only for posts that have no nationality rule attached to them

questions.hint: Right to work is a legal requirement; nationality rules are an additional eligibility requirement.

questions.prompt: An employee's immigration status changes during employment. What is appropriate?

options.text: Tell the employer promptly and provide updated evidence
Wait to be asked by the employer, then explain what happened and when it took place
Say nothing if the change looks small, as the employer will find out at the next scheduled check
Ask a colleague to deal with it for them, since a change of status is a private personal matter

questions.hint: Staff should be open about changes that affect the right to work.

questions.prompt: An employee has applied to extend their permission before it expires. What should the employer do?

options.text: Carry on as normal and never check again, because an application is the same as permission
Ask them to stop work unpaid until a decision is made, whatever the guidance says
Dismiss them on the expiry date automatically, as the permission no longer covers the work
Follow the Home Office guidance for that situation instead of assuming either way

questions.hint: Applying in time can affect what an employer may do, so official guidance should be followed.

questions.prompt: What should the employer keep after a right to work check?

options.text: An email from the employee's previous employer confirming their previous employment and its dates
A dated record of the check that was carried out, stored securely and kept for as long as the rules require
A copy of the employee's bank statement, which shows that they are living in the UK
Nothing, because the check is a verbal one and leaves no paperwork to be stored

questions.hint: A dated record shows the check was done properly.

questions.prompt: Which statement about being asked to prove the right to work is correct?

options.text: It only happens when the employer has some doubt about the person's status or background
It is optional for the employer if the person speaks with a UK accent and has lived locally
It is performed by the Home Office on the employer's behalf, so the employer takes no part
It is a routine legal check on everyone and not an accusation

questions.hint: The check is routine and applies to all new employees.

items.title: L6: Matching nationality rules to adverts
items.source: Civil Service Nationality Rules (GOV.UK); Civil Service Jobs
items.body:
Nationality rules set out which nationalities are eligible to work in the Civil Service and in which roles. They are separate from right to work and from security clearance. A person might meet one and not the other. All three can apply to the same job.

In very broad terms, many posts are open to UK nationals and citizens of some other countries, such as Commonwealth and Irish citizens, and to people with certain immigration permissions. Some posts, often those involving national security, are reserved to UK nationals or to people with a specific status. The details change over time, so the authoritative source is the eligibility statement in each advert, which is written for that job.

The statement is read literally. If it says, 'This post is open to UK nationals only', then holding another nationality as the only one makes you ineligible, however qualified you are. If it says 'open to UK, Commonwealth and Irish nationals', then a Commonwealth citizen can apply. If it refers to 'single or dual nationality', read what is meant and ask if it is not clear. Dual nationality can matter: holding another nationality besides UK may be fine for some posts, and may be a factor in security vetting for others.

Before applying, check eligibility, not just suitability. If you are unsure, use the contact in the advert before you spend time on the application. Do not assume that a colleague's route applies to you: rules depend on your own status.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the relationship between nationality rules, right to work and clearance?

options.text: They are three separate requirements, each answering a different question, and a single job may involve all of them
They are applied in sequence, so that passing the first one cancels the need for the others
They are one requirement known by three different names in different departments
They apply only to jobs in the security services and do not matter elsewhere in the Civil Service

questions.hint: Each addresses a different question, and a job can involve all of them.

questions.prompt: An advert says 'open to UK nationals only'. Anika holds only Canadian citizenship and has excellent skills. What is her position?

options.text: She can apply if she has lived in the UK for many years, since long residence counts as UK status
She can apply if she is clearly the best candidate, because skills outweigh nationality in selection
She is not eligible for this post, however strong her skills
She can apply if a manager recommends her, because recommendations can waive the eligibility statement

questions.hint: The eligibility statement is applied literally; skills do not override it.

questions.prompt: An advert is open to 'UK, Commonwealth and Irish nationals'. Joseph is an Irish citizen. What is the position?

options.text: He is automatically cleared for any security level, because his nationality is on the list of those accepted
He cannot apply, because the Irish nationals who are named are only those living in Northern Ireland
He meets the nationality statement, but he still has to show the right to work and pass any clearance the role needs
He must first obtain UK citizenship, since the statement allows only people who hold a UK passport

questions.hint: Nationality is one requirement; other checks still apply.

questions.prompt: Why should you read the eligibility statement before preparing an application?

options.text: It lists the skills that will be tested at interview, so that you can prepare your answers in advance
It tells you whether you may apply for that specific job, which saves wasted effort
It shows the names of the other candidates, so you can see how strong the competition is
It tells you the pay band you will be offered if you are successful at the end of the process

questions.hint: The statement is job-specific and decides eligibility before suitability.

questions.prompt: A colleague from another country joined last year in a similar grade. Aisha assumes the same route applies to her. What is the flaw?

options.text: Rules depend on each person's own status and the specific post, so she must check for herself
There is no flaw, because the colleague's route is recorded on the advert for anyone to rely upon
There is no flaw, because the rules are the same for every role in the Civil Service at a given grade
The flaw is that colleagues never share any information about how they were recruited

questions.hint: Eligibility depends on individual status and the post, not on what someone else did.

questions.prompt: Why can dual nationality matter?

options.text: It speeds up security clearance, because it shows the person has links to more than one country
It affects only pay, because the second nationality may attract a different allowance
It bars a person from every Civil Service post, whatever the role and whatever the other nationality
It may be acceptable for some posts, while for others the second nationality may be considered during vetting

questions.hint: Dual nationality can be considered, particularly in vetting for sensitive roles.

questions.prompt: What is the best action if an eligibility statement is unclear to you?

options.text: Use the contact in the advert before applying
Apply anyway and see what happens, since eligibility can be sorted out after the application
Post the question on social media, where other applicants can answer for you
Ask a friend who works in another department, because they will know the rules for every post

questions.hint: The advert contact can clarify an unclear statement for that job.

questions.prompt: Which reason most plausibly explains why a role is reserved to UK nationals?

options.text: The role pays more than other posts, so UK nationals are given priority for the higher salary
The role has a shorter notice period, which suits people who are already living in the UK
The work involves matters where the government needs particular assurance, such as national security
The role is a temporary placement, and such placements are never offered to other nationals

questions.hint: Reservations usually reflect national security or similar assurance reasons.

questions.prompt: Cora meets the nationality rule and has the right to work, but the role needs SC clearance. What does she still need?

options.text: Nothing further, because meeting nationality and right to work rules means clearance is given with them
A new passport, because SC clearance can only be granted against a passport issued in the last year
A reference from the chief executive of a previous employer, who must vouch for her in person
A successful vetting decision at SC level, which is a separate step from nationality and right to work

questions.hint: Clearance is a separate step even where the other requirements are met.

questions.prompt: Why do nationality rules exist for some posts?

options.text: To reduce the number of applications, which makes the selection process quicker for recruiting managers
To protect the government's trust and security in sensitive work
To create more roles for graduates, who are given priority in the posts that are open to UK nationals
To make the recruitment process longer, so that only the most committed candidates are left

questions.hint: Rules reflect a need for assurance in sensitive work.

items.title: L6: Choosing the right clearance level
items.source: HMG Personnel Security Controls (GOV.UK); UK Security Vetting (UKSV)
items.body:
The Civil Service uses four main levels. The Baseline Personnel Security Standard is the foundation and is not a formal clearance but a set of checks for almost everyone. Counter Terrorist Check (CTC) adds criminal record, security service and credit checks for roles with unsupervised access to certain sites or with proximity to people at risk. Security Check (SC) is for roles with regular access to SECRET material, or with occasional access to TOP SECRET. Developed Vetting (DV) is the highest and is for roles with frequent and uncontrolled access to TOP SECRET or for other particularly sensitive work. Vetting is carried out for most departments by UK Security Vetting (UKSV).

The level is set by the role, not the person and not the grade. A junior post that handles SECRET material may need SC, while a senior post that handles only OFFICIAL material may need only the baseline. The sponsoring department decides which level the role needs, based on the sensitivity of the assets, the access, and the context. Each higher level builds on the checks below it, and looks at more of your life and for longer.

The level also affects timing and burden. DV takes longest and involves an interview and checks with referees. A department should ask for the lowest level that does the job, because vetting costs time and money, and intrusive checks should be proportionate.

A clearance is granted for a purpose. If you move to a role needing a higher level, a new application is required. A clearance that is not used for a time may lapse or need review.

questions.prompt: A junior caseworker in a records team regularly handles SECRET material as part of the job. Which level is the role most likely to be given?

options.text: DV, because any SECRET material requires the highest level of vetting available
CTC, because it is the usual level for anything that falls short of DV
SC, because regular access to SECRET material is the usual case that level is designed to cover
Baseline only, because a junior grade cannot need more than the baseline checks

questions.hint: The level follows the access the role needs; regular SECRET access points to SC.

questions.prompt: Why might a senior policy post need nothing above the baseline checks?

options.text: The level depends on the access the role needs, and a post handling only OFFICIAL material may need no more
Senior staff are exempt from vetting once they have passed their first probation period
Seniority raises the level, so senior posts always need the highest level of clearance on offer
The baseline is the only level available to anyone above a certain grade, so nothing higher is possible

questions.hint: Clearance is tied to the role's access, not its seniority.

questions.prompt: Who decides which clearance level a particular role needs?

options.text: UKSV, which sets a level for every job as soon as it is advertised on Civil Service Jobs
The candidate's current employer, based on the person's reputation and length of service
The candidate, who picks the level on the application form to match their own experience
The sponsoring department, based on the sensitivity of the access the role involves

questions.hint: The employing department sponsors the clearance and sets the level for the role.

questions.prompt: What is the role of UK Security Vetting (UKSV) in the process?

options.text: It decides which applicants will be invited to interview for the post
It carries out the vetting for most departments once a sponsor requests it
It sets pay and grade for the posts that need clearance
It writes the job adverts that state the clearance level for each post

questions.hint: UKSV does the vetting work; the department sponsors and decides the need.

questions.prompt: Why should a department ask for the lowest level of clearance that meets the need?

options.text: Lower levels are more reliable, because they use fewer sources and so make fewer errors
Vetting is intrusive and costs time and money, so it should be proportionate to the risk
Candidates are more likely to accept an offer if the level is low, which helps recruitment
Higher levels are not available to most departments, which must therefore use the lower ones

questions.hint: Proportionality is a principle: ask for no more than the role requires.

questions.prompt: Which feature is typical of DV but not of the lower levels?

options.text: An interview and checks with referees as part of a more thorough process
Questions about previous employers and the dates of employment
A check on the right to work in the UK before the person starts
A check of the person's identity documents against the original records

questions.hint: DV is the most thorough level and normally includes an interview and referee contact.

questions.prompt: A role gives unsupervised access to a government site that could be a terrorist target, but involves no SECRET material. Which level fits best?

options.text: The baseline checks alone, because the site contains no SECRET material at all
DV, because anything linked to terrorism needs the highest level
CTC, which is aimed at unsupervised access to sensitive sites rather than at SECRET material
SC, because unsupervised access always requires access to SECRET material

questions.hint: CTC is aimed at unsupervised access to sensitive sites or proximity to people at risk.

questions.prompt: Joel holds SC and applies for a role that needs DV. What does he need to do?

options.text: Do nothing, as his existing SC already covers every role that needs DV
Ask his manager to approve the move informally, which is enough to extend his clearance
Update his address records with the vetting service, which will then raise his level
Go through a fresh application for the higher level

questions.hint: A higher level means a new vetting application, though earlier checks may be reused.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a clearance that has not been used for a long time is the most accurate?

options.text: It may lapse or need a review before the holder can rely on it again in a new post
It stays valid indefinitely wherever the holder works, whether it is used or not
It becomes a higher level over time, because the holder's record has become longer
It passes to the next holder of the same job, who benefits from it

questions.hint: Clearance is time-limited and granted for a purpose, so unused clearance may need renewing.

questions.prompt: What does 'each level builds on the one below' mean in practice?

options.text: CTC and SC are two names for the same check, used in different departments
Baseline checks are repeated only for DV, and are not part of the other levels
DV replaces every other check, so the lower checks are not done for people who hold it
Someone cleared to SC will already have been through the baseline checks

questions.hint: Higher levels include and extend the checks below them.

items.title: L6: Completing the security questionnaire
items.source: UK Security Vetting guidance; HMG Personnel Security Controls (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Clearance above the baseline starts with a security questionnaire, usually completed online after the department sponsors you. It asks about your personal details, addresses, employment, finances, family and close associates, foreign travel and contacts, and any past conduct that might matter. Higher levels ask for more detail and a longer period of history.

Vetting is about trust, reliability and vulnerability. It asks whether you are honest, whether you can be relied on to protect information, and whether anything in your life could make you open to pressure or coercion. Having debts, a relative abroad or a past mistake does not by itself rule you out. Concealing them is what causes the real damage, because it suggests you may hide things later. Vetting staff would rather read an honest account of a problem than discover it from another source.

Complete the form carefully. Collect information before you start: addresses with dates, employers, the people you will name as referees or associates, and details of any foreign travel or contacts. Where you do not know something exactly, say so and give a best estimate. Do not leave blanks, and do not answer on the assumption that something is too small to matter. If in doubt, include it and explain.

Referees and associates may be contacted. Tell them beforehand so they are ready, and so that you know they are willing. Incomplete or inaccurate forms are returned or delayed, and an inaccurate form can lead to a refusal.

questions.prompt: Which set of questions best summarises what vetting tries to establish?

options.text: Whether you are well qualified, popular with colleagues and likely to be promoted
Whether you are honest, can be relied on with information, and are not open to pressure
Whether you share the political views of the government of the day and support its policies
Whether you are in good health, living near the office and free of any kind of debt

questions.hint: Vetting is about honesty, reliability and vulnerability to coercion.

questions.prompt: Dina has run up credit card debt which she is repaying. How should she treat it on the questionnaire?

options.text: Leave it out, since everyone has some debt and it will be ignored by the vetting team
Leave it out until she has repaid it in full, when it will no longer be relevant
Declare it honestly with the details, since it is concealment rather than ordinary debt that would cause the real damage
Declare it only if the vetting team asks her about it in person, since the form does not require it

questions.hint: Ordinary debt does not rule people out; hiding it signals a willingness to conceal.

questions.prompt: Ayo's brother lives abroad and Ayo is unsure whether to list him. What is the sensible approach?

options.text: Leave him out unless the form names his country, as other countries are not asked about
List him only if they speak every week, since only regular contact matters to the vetting team
Leave him out, because family living abroad is never relevant to a security questionnaire
List him and add a short explanation, since doubt is a reason to include

questions.hint: If in doubt, include and explain; vetting staff decide what matters.

questions.prompt: Which preparation is most useful before opening the online questionnaire?

options.text: Reading the Official Secrets Act in full, so that you understand the legal position
Gathering dated addresses, employers, referee details and travel information
Asking a friend to fill it in for you so that it is done quickly and correctly
Waiting for a reminder from the vetting team before you make a start on it

questions.hint: Having the information to hand reduces errors and delay.

questions.prompt: You cannot recall exactly when you moved into a flat three years ago. What is best?

options.text: Leave the date blank because you cannot be certain, and let the vetting team fill the gap
Put a precise date you think is probably right, as a firm date looks more reliable
Check tenancy or bank records to firm it up, or give a best estimate and mark it clearly as approximate
Skip the address altogether and tell them about it later in the process if they ask

questions.hint: Flagged estimates are acceptable; blanks and false precision are not.

questions.prompt: Why should you contact your referees before naming them?

options.text: They may be approached, so they need to know and be willing to respond
They have to work in the same department as you, so you should check this first
They must sign your questionnaire before it is submitted to the vetting service
They have to pay a fee to be listed, which you must agree with them in advance

questions.hint: Referees can be contacted, and unprepared referees slow things down.

questions.prompt: What usually happens to an incomplete questionnaire?

options.text: It is returned or held up until the gaps are filled, so the whole process is delayed
It is passed on to a lower clearance level, which asks fewer questions
It is accepted as it stands, and the gaps are treated as meaning there is nothing to report
It is held until the next annual vetting window, when the missing sections can be added

questions.hint: Incomplete forms slow the process and may be sent back.

questions.prompt: Why is a hidden problem often judged more seriously than the problem itself?

options.text: Hiding a problem is automatically a criminal offence under the Official Secrets Act
It suggests the person may hide things in future, which undermines trust
Hidden problems are always larger than the ones that people disclose on the form
The vetting team has no way of judging a problem that the person discloses openly

questions.hint: Trust and honesty are at the heart of vetting.

questions.prompt: You think a small matter is 'too small to matter'. What is the right call on the form?

options.text: Wait to see whether it comes up later in the process before deciding whether to declare it
Leave it out to keep the form short, since vetting staff are busy and want only the important points
Mention it only if you are asked at the interview, when you can judge how serious it is
Include it with a short explanation if you have any doubt, and let the vetting team decide whether it matters

questions.hint: Vetting staff decide what matters; the applicant should disclose when in doubt.

questions.prompt: Which description of the questionnaire is correct?

options.text: It asks only about criminal convictions and nothing about other parts of a person's life
It is a general knowledge test taken under timed conditions on an approved device
It covers history, finances, associates and contacts, with more detail at higher levels
It is identical for every clearance level, so the same form is used throughout

questions.hint: Scope and depth grow with the level of clearance.

items.title: L6: Classifications and handling day to day
items.body:
The Government Security Classifications Policy has three levels: OFFICIAL, SECRET and TOP SECRET. Most government work is OFFICIAL. Information is classified by the harm that would follow if it were lost or disclosed. A further marking, OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE, is used for some OFFICIAL information that needs extra care, for example because it contains personal data or commercial secrets. It is a handling marking rather than a fourth classification.

Handling rules follow the classification and the need to know. You should only see or share information if your work requires it, whatever your clearance. Good everyday habits include locking your screen when you leave your desk, not leaving papers where others can read them, not discussing work in public places, and using approved systems and devices. You should not forward work information to personal email, and you should not use personal messaging apps for official business unless policy allows it.

Physical handling also matters: collect printing promptly, store papers in locked storage when away, use secure disposal, and take care when carrying documents. When sending sensitive information, check the recipient, use the approved method, and apply marking where policy requires. If you receive information not meant for you, tell the sender and do not use or share it.

If you make a mistake, such as sending an email to the wrong person or losing a document, report it straight away through your department's process. Early reporting allows damage to be limited. Departments generally prefer prompt honest reports to concealed errors.

questions.prompt: How should OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE be understood?

options.text: As another name for SECRET, used in departments that prefer the older term
As a handling marking for some OFFICIAL information that needs extra care
As a marking used on documents that have already been released to the public
As a fourth classification level that sits above TOP SECRET in the policy

questions.hint: It is a handling caveat within OFFICIAL, not a separate classification level.

questions.prompt: What is a classification based on?

options.text: The length and format of the document, since longer documents hold more detail
The number of people who have already seen it, since wide circulation raises the risk
The harm that would follow if the information were lost or disclosed
The grade of the person who wrote it, because senior authors handle more serious matters

questions.hint: Classification reflects the potential harm from compromise.

questions.prompt: Ravi has high clearance and is curious about a project outside his work. May he read its files?

options.text: He may read it if the project is in the same building as his team and he has a valid pass
He may read it provided he reads only the summary page and not the detailed supporting papers
His clearance gives him access to everything at or below that level, so he may read what he likes
Only if his work requires it, because need to know applies as well as clearance

questions.hint: Clearance never replaces the need to know.

questions.prompt: Mia wants to finish work at home and thinks of forwarding a spreadsheet of customer details to her personal email. What is correct?

options.text: Do not forward it to a personal account; use approved systems or ask her manager how she can work securely from home
Forward only the first sheet she needs, since a partial copy carries less risk than the whole file
Forward it if her personal account has a strong password, since the password protects the data
Forward it, then delete it from her personal account the next morning once the work is finished

questions.hint: Official information should stay on approved systems.

questions.prompt: A colleague prints a sensitive paper and leaves it on the printer for an hour. What is wrong with this?

options.text: It is only a problem if the colleague is senior, since only senior staff handle sensitive papers
Nothing, if the paper is only an internal document and not one that is sent to customers
Nothing, because paper is lower risk than digital copies and is rarely read by anyone passing
Others could read or take it, so print-outs should be collected promptly

questions.hint: Uncollected print-outs are a common source of accidental disclosure.

questions.prompt: You receive an email containing another team's personal data, sent to you by mistake. What do you do?

options.text: Forward it to the intended team yourself, since this puts the mistake right as quickly as possible
Tell the sender about the mistake and do not use or share the information
Delete it and say nothing, as it is not your business and reporting it would only cause trouble
Keep it in a folder in case it turns out to be useful for your own work later

questions.hint: Misdirected information should be reported back so the error can be dealt with.

questions.prompt: Why should an accidental disclosure be reported straight away?

options.text: Early reporting lets the department limit the damage
So that the person responsible can be disciplined as quickly as possible
Because later reports are not accepted, however good the reason for the delay
Because the report must be filed before the end of the month in which it happened

questions.hint: Prompt reports allow containment and recovery.

questions.prompt: Which place is least suitable for a conversation about a work matter involving personal data?

options.text: A closed meeting room, because the door might be left unlocked by someone else
A quiet corner of the office kitchen, because the sink and kettle are close by
A crowded commuter train, where other passengers could overhear or see a screen
An approved secure video call, because the other participants could repeat what was said

questions.hint: Public places risk being overheard.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the classification levels is right?

options.text: There are five levels, running from PUBLIC through to CRITICAL
There are three levels: OFFICIAL, SECRET and TOP SECRET
Each department chooses its own set of levels to suit the work that it does
There are two levels, OFFICIAL and SECRET, with TOP SECRET used only by the agencies

questions.hint: The policy has three levels.

questions.prompt: Why might OFFICIAL information be given the OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE marking?

options.text: It contains something, such as personal data or commercial detail, that needs extra care
It has not yet been checked for spelling and accuracy, so it must be treated cautiously
It is older than a year, and older documents need more care when they are handled
It was written by a senior manager, whose documents attract the extra marking

questions.hint: The marking flags extra handling for particularly sensitive OFFICIAL material.

items.title: L6: Everyday scenarios and the Official Secrets Act
items.source: Official Secrets Act 1989 (legislation.gov.uk); Civil Service Code; National Security Act 2023
items.body:
The Official Secrets Act 1989 makes it a criminal offence for a Crown servant to make a damaging unauthorised disclosure of certain official information. The categories include security and intelligence, defence, international relations, and information that could help commit crime or impede its detection. The Act applies to Crown servants, which includes civil servants, and also to government contractors and to people who have been notified. The obligation continues after you leave. The 1989 Act does not contain a public interest defence. The National Security Act 2023 now covers espionage, sabotage and foreign interference.

Most everyday work is not covered by those categories, but you still owe confidentiality. The Civil Service Code requires integrity and honesty, and you must not misuse official information or disclose it without authority. Departments usually ask new staff to sign a declaration acknowledging the Act.

In practice, the issue arises in ordinary situations: a conversation with a friend about what you do, a post on social media about your department, a book or article after you leave, or contact from a journalist. In each case, the correct approach is to speak to the press office or your line manager before saying anything about official work, and not to disclose anything you are not authorised to. Describing your general role in a non-sensitive way is normally fine.

If you believe something wrong is happening, there are proper routes for raising a concern, such as your line manager, a nominated officer, or ultimately the Civil Service Commission, rather than disclosing to the press.

questions.prompt: A journalist phones you about your department's work. What is the correct response?

options.text: Give your view but ask not to be named, which keeps you safe and still helps the story
Answer informally if the question seems harmless, since helpful staff build good press relations
Refer them to the press office and tell your line manager about the call
Offer to email documents so the journalist can check the facts for themselves

questions.hint: Press contact is handled by the press office, not by individual staff.

questions.prompt: Does the Official Secrets Act 1989 still apply once you have left the Civil Service?

options.text: The obligation continues for the first year after leaving and then lapses
The obligation ends on your last day, because it applies only to people currently employed
The obligation continues only if you move to a government contractor after leaving
The obligation continues after you leave

questions.hint: The duty of confidentiality survives the end of employment.

questions.prompt: What is the position on a public interest defence under the 1989 Act?

options.text: The Act contains one if the information was already available somewhere online
The Act contains one for senior staff only, who can judge the wider public interest
The Act contains one for all disclosures made to the press, provided they are accurate
The Act does not contain a public interest defence, so a belief that disclosure was justified is no defence

questions.hint: The 1989 Act has no public interest defence.

questions.prompt: Ben plans to write a book about his department after he retires. What is the right first step?

options.text: Seek approval or advice from the department, since official information is still protected
Publish under a pen name without telling anyone, so that nothing can be traced to him
Publish it so long as the book is described as fiction, since fiction is not covered
Publish it freely, as he no longer works there and his duties ended on retirement

questions.hint: Duties continue after leaving, so advice should be sought before publishing.

questions.prompt: A friend asks what project you worked on this week. What is the best answer?

options.text: Refuse to speak about your work at all, in any form, since any mention is forbidden
Give a full account, as a friend can be trusted and will not repeat it to anyone
Describe your role in general terms without sensitive detail
Show them your work on your phone, as that is more honest than describing it

questions.hint: General descriptions are fine; sensitive detail is not.

questions.prompt: You believe your department is acting improperly. Which route is right?

options.text: Tell a journalist first, so that the story cannot be buried by the department
Raise it through your line manager, a nominated officer or the Civil Service Commission route
Post it on social media to apply pressure, because public attention is the fastest way to get action
Delete the files so they cannot be used for the improper purpose

questions.hint: Established internal and independent routes exist for raising concerns.

questions.prompt: Which is a recognised category of information under the 1989 Act?

options.text: Published weather statistics, because they are produced by a government body
Defence, which sits alongside security and intelligence and international relations as a protected category
Staff social events, because they involve the movement of government staff
Office stationery orders, because they show how public money is spent

questions.hint: Defence is one of the protected categories, alongside security and international relations.

questions.prompt: What does the National Security Act 2023 deal with?

options.text: Public sector pensions and the rules for early retirement of staff
Planning applications for new government buildings and their security fencing
Parking and traffic offences on government land and in government car parks
Espionage, sabotage and foreign interference

questions.hint: It modernised offences concerning state threats.

questions.prompt: Who is covered by the 1989 Act?

options.text: Only people who have signed a form, since the Act depends on their agreement
Only ministers, as they are the people who take the final decisions in government
Crown servants, government contractors and other people who have been formally notified that the Act applies to them
Only staff in the intelligence agencies, because other departments hold no protected material

questions.hint: The Act applies widely, not just to specific agencies.

questions.prompt: What does the declaration new staff often sign actually do?

options.text: It records that they understand the Act applies to them
It replaces the contract of employment in the matter of confidentiality and secrecy
It makes the Act apply to them for the first time, as they were not covered before signing
It waives the Act for ordinary work, so that only special material is protected

questions.hint: The Act applies by law; the declaration records awareness.

items.title: L6: Conflicts of interest, gifts and outside activity
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code; Bribery Act 2010
items.body:
A conflict of interest arises when your private interests, or those of someone close to you, could affect, or appear to affect, how you do your job. It does not need to involve wrongdoing: the appearance matters too. Examples include a relative bidding for a contract you help to award, a second job with a supplier, a financial interest in a company your team regulates, or a close friendship with someone who is an applicant.

The standard approach is to declare early, to your line manager or through the department's process, and let them decide how to manage it. Management can include removing you from a decision, changing your duties, or recording the interest on a register. Declaring is not an admission of fault. Failing to declare is the problem.

Gifts and hospitality follow the same logic. Civil servants should not accept anything that might influence, or look as if it influences, their decisions. Departments set rules and usually require you to record offers, including ones you refuse. Small items of token value may be acceptable under local rules, but cash is not, and nothing should be accepted from a supplier during a live procurement. The Bribery Act 2010 makes it an offence to offer, give, request or accept a bribe.

Outside activity, such as a second job, voluntary role or business interest, usually needs approval. Political activity is also restricted: the rules vary by grade and role, with more senior and sensitive posts more restricted. Always check before taking public political roles.

questions.prompt: Your sister's company is bidding for a contract you help to evaluate. What should you do?

options.text: Ask her to keep quiet about the connection until the contract has been awarded
Declare it to your manager straight away and expect to step back from the decision
Say nothing, because she works for a different organisation and you gain no direct benefit
Score her bid fairly and keep the relationship private, since fair scoring removes any concern

questions.hint: Declare early and let the department manage it, usually by removing you from the decision.

questions.prompt: Does a conflict of interest require actual wrongdoing?

options.text: It counts only where money has changed hands between the parties concerned
It matters only for senior staff, since junior staff cannot influence decisions
There must be proof of fraud before a situation is treated as a conflict
The appearance of a conflict can also damage trust, so a conflict does not need proof of wrongdoing

questions.hint: Perceived conflicts matter as well as actual ones.

questions.prompt: A supplier in a live procurement offers you a boxed gift. What is the right response?

options.text: Accept it and keep it at home, since a private gift is not connected to your work
Accept it if it is small, since small gifts do not influence decisions
Decline it and record the offer in line with local rules
Accept it and share it with the team, which makes it a team gift rather than a personal one

questions.hint: Gifts from a supplier in a live procurement should not be accepted.

questions.prompt: What does declaring a conflict of interest signal?

options.text: That you are acting properly and openly, and it is not an admission of fault of any kind
That you are asking for special treatment from your manager in the decision
That you have already done something wrong and are trying to put it right
That you want to be moved to another team, away from the work in question

questions.hint: Declaring is the correct step, not a confession.

questions.prompt: Why are declined gifts often recorded as well?

options.text: So that the giver can claim the cost back as an expense from the department
The records show openness and help spot patterns of approaches
Because refusing a gift is a breach of the code, and breaches have to be logged
So the gift can be collected later if the person who offered it makes a complaint

questions.hint: Departments usually want offers recorded, including ones refused.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the Bribery Act 2010 is correct?

options.text: It makes offering, giving, requesting or accepting a bribe an offence, which covers both sides of the exchange
It applies only to the private sector and does not cover people working in the public sector
It applies only to ministers, who take the decisions on which bribes would be offered
It applies only to cash payments, so gifts of other kinds fall outside its scope

questions.hint: The Act is wide in scope and covers both giving and taking.

questions.prompt: You want a weekend job with a company that does business with your department. What should you do?

options.text: Start the job and mention it at your next review, once you know whether you like it
Take the job under a different name, since the company would not know your department
Seek approval and declare the potential conflict before you start
Take the job but decline any pay, since unpaid work cannot create a conflict

questions.hint: Outside activity usually needs approval, especially where a link exists.

questions.prompt: How are rules on political activity usually structured?

options.text: They are identical for every member of staff, whatever their grade and role
They do not exist for civil servants, who are free to act as they choose in their own time
They apply only to ministers, since civil servants do not take part in politics
They vary by grade and role, with more restrictions on senior and sensitive posts

questions.hint: The Management Code sets graded restrictions.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a common way to manage a declared conflict?

options.text: Promoting the person so that they are no longer involved at the same level
Ignoring the declaration unless somebody makes a complaint about the decision
Closing the case, because declaring it has already put the matter right
Removing the person from the decision, or changing their duties so that the interest cannot affect it

questions.hint: Managing the conflict can include removal from the decision or changed duties.

questions.prompt: Which interest could create a conflict for someone working in a regulator?

options.text: A financial stake in a company that the team regulates
